teaser: He once had a roof over his head. The sea took it, and he has sat in the rain ever since.
review_notes:
Image is small, panoramic and heavily processed (HDR): interactive blocks point only at large regions.
Funding by donations gathered by the priest Joko and the court lady Inada no Tsubone; earlier wooden statue completed 1243 and damaged by a storm in 1248; bronze begun 1252.
Casters' names traditionally given as Ono Goroemon and/or Tanji Hisatomo (left out of lesson as uncertain).
Height about 11.3 m (13.35 m with base), weight about 121 tons.
Hall destroyed by storms in 1334 and 1369 and by a tsunami in 1498 (date and cause debated by historians).
Base work after the 1923 earthquake and the 1960-61 reinforcement of the neck.
Interior visit fee (a few tens of yen) may have changed.

lesson.text: In 1252 the bronze casters of Kamakura took on a job that had no royal budget behind it. The statue was paid for coin by coin, with donations that a priest named Jōkō had spent years collecting from ordinary people, helped by a lady of the court. Their first attempt, a giant Buddha of wood, had been wrecked by a storm only a few years earlier.

So this time they chose bronze. Kamakura was then the seat of the shoguns, the military rulers of Japan, and a young, ambitious capital. A colossal Buddha would show that it could rival the old cities of Nara and Kyoto.

The figure is Amida, the Buddha of Infinite Light, who in Japanese belief welcomes the faithful into his paradise after death. He sits about 11.3 meters high (37 feet) without the base and weighs around 121 tons.
Numbers are hard to feel. Find the visitors in this photo to get the scale.

spots.title: Under umbrellas
spots.text: A few people cross the wet courtyard. Stand one of them next to the statue: they would barely reach above the stone base, far below the Buddha's knees.

lesson.text: A bronze that size cannot be poured in one go. The casters built it from the ground up in horizontal layers, raising the mold and pouring each new band onto the one below. The seams between pours are still visible on the surface, like growth rings.
The statue is hollow, and for a small coin you can walk inside it. From there you see the grid of joints left by the casting, and two windows cut into the back.

The Buddha was not meant to sit under the sky. A great wooden hall once enclosed him. Storms brought it down in the 1300s, and it was rebuilt. Then, according to temple tradition, a tsunami in 1498 swept the building away for good. The bronze did not move.
The Great Buddha of Kamakura became an outdoor monument by accident. Its weathered green skin and open sky were never part of the plan.

That accident changed how the sculpture is seen. Indoors, visitors would have stood close, in dim light, craning their necks. The sculptors planned for that viewpoint, and it explains several oddities you can check for yourself.

spots.title: A head that leans
spots.text: The head is large for the body and tilts forward. From the ground this corrects the perspective, and brings the lowered gaze down to meet yours.

spots.title: Snail-shell curls
spots.text: The hair is a cap of tight coils, a traditional mark of a Buddha. Each curl was cast as a small spiral bump.

spots.title: Robes like water
spots.text: The robe falls from both shoulders in long parallel folds that spill over the lap. Their regular rhythm adds to the stillness.

spots.title: Hands in the lap
spots.text: The hands rest together in his lap, palms up. This is the gesture of meditation that identifies Amida.

spots.title: The stone base
spots.text: A low platform of cut blocks. It was reworked after the great earthquake of 1923 shook the statue.

spots.title: The cloister
spots.text: Tiled roofs of the covered walkway that rings the courtyard. They give no shelter to the Buddha himself.

lesson.text: The color is another gift of the weather. Bronze turns green as its copper reacts with air and rain, forming a crust called a patina. Originally the statue was gilded, and faint traces of gold still cling around the cheeks.
The Buddha has ridden out many earthquakes. In the early 1960s engineers reinforced the neck and reworked the base so the statue can slide slightly during a tremor instead of cracking.

Foreign travelers of the 1800s were deeply struck by this calm figure seated among trees. The British writer Rudyard Kipling visited in 1892 and wove verses about “the Buddha at Kamakura” into his novel Kim.
Hanging in the temple grounds is a pair of giant straw sandals, close to two meters long, woven by children so that the Buddha could walk around Japan if he wished.

Return to the photo: rain is falling, umbrellas hurry past, and he has not stirred. The people who gave their coins in the 1240s wanted a Buddha that a storm could not destroy. They got one that has outlasted every roof built to protect it.

quiz.question: How was the Great Buddha paid for?
options: By donations collected from ordinary people
quiz.explanation: A priest gathered donations over years.

quiz.question: Why does the Buddha sit outdoors today?
options: Its hall was destroyed and never rebuilt
It was designed as a garden statue
It was moved out for tourists
quiz.explanation: Storms and then a tsunami removed the wooden hall.

quiz.question: Why does the bronze look green?
options: Copper in the bronze reacts with air and rain
quiz.explanation: The green crust is a natural patina.

quiz.question: Which Buddha does the statue represent?
options: The historical Buddha as a child
quiz.explanation: It shows Amida, with hands in the meditation gesture.

quiz.question: Why does the head tilt forward and look large?
options: It was damaged in an earthquake
To look right to viewers standing below
The casters ran out of bronze
quiz.explanation: The proportions correct for a viewpoint from the ground.

facts.text: The statue is solid bronze all the way through.
facts.explanation: It is hollow, and visitors can go inside.

facts.text: A wooden Buddha came before the bronze one and was wrecked by a storm.
facts.explanation: That loss led to the choice of bronze in 1252.

facts.text: The statue was cast in a single pour.
facts.explanation: It was built up in horizontal layers, and the seams still show.
